messages.content: Can you help me make Cupids Cookies? I’ve got a medium mixing bowl out and want to make sure I start correctly.
Absolutely. Set out 1 cup butter and 1 cup white sugar so they can be creamed together smoothly. If the butter is softened, it’ll be much easier to get that light, fluffy texture.
The butter is soft and the sugar is measured. Do I need anything else before mixing?
Yes—have 1 egg and 1 1/2 teaspoons vanilla extract ready too. You’ll use those right after the butter and sugar are creamed.
Okay, the egg and vanilla are beside the bowl. Should I use a mixer or do this by hand?
Either works, but a hand mixer will make it faster. Cream the butter and white sugar in the medium bowl until the mixture looks pale, lighter in texture, and fluffy rather than dense.
It’s looking creamy and a little fluffy now. Should the egg go in all at once?
Yes, blend in the egg, then add the vanilla extract. Mix until everything is combined and the batter looks smooth.
The wet mixture is smooth. I noticed the directions mention flour and salt—what do I do with those?
Sift the flour and salt together in a separate bowl before adding them. The recipe doesn’t list exact amounts for those, so use the amounts from your recipe card or package notes if you have them.
I’ve sifted them together. Should I dump it all in or add it slowly?
Add the sifted flour and salt to the creamed mixture gradually if you can, mixing as you go. That helps prevent dry pockets and keeps the dough more even.
The dough is coming together. How mixed should it be before I stop?
Stop once the dry ingredients are fully incorporated and the dough looks uniform. Give the bowl a quick scrape along the sides and bottom, then mix just enough to bring everything together well.
I’m making Garden Party Salad and want to get the dressing started. What should I pull out first?
Set out a small bowl and a whisk. For the dressing ingredients listed, you’ll need 1/4 cup vegetable oil, 1/4 cup orange marmalade, 3 tablespoons cider vinegar, and 3 tablespoons mayonnaise.
I’ve got the oil and marmalade measured. Should the marmalade go in as-is, or do I need to warm it?
Use it as-is unless it’s very stiff. Add the orange marmalade to the bowl with the vegetable oil, then whisk firmly so it starts loosening into the oil.
Okay, the marmalade is breaking up. I’m adding the cider vinegar and mayo now—what texture am I looking for?
Whisk until the dressing looks smooth and cohesive, with no obvious streaks of mayonnaise or clumps of marmalade. Once it’s smooth, put it in the refrigerator to chill.
The dressing is chilling. Should I mix the salad base now or wait?
Wait until just before serving. That keeps the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley from sitting too long in the dressing.
I’m close to serving. What bowl should I use for the chicken mixture?
Use a large bowl so there’s room to toss without spilling. Add the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley to that bowl.
Everything is in the large bowl. Do I pour in all the chilled dressing at once?
Add the chilled dressing over the chicken mixture, then toss gently but thoroughly so the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley are evenly coated.
It looks coated. Any serving or cleanup tips before I bring it out?
Give it one final light toss right before it goes to the table. Wipe the rim of the serving bowl if needed, and keep it chilled until serving time.
Can you help me make Chicken and Black Bean Chili? I’ve got a large pot out and want to stay on track.
Absolutely. Set up 2 tablespoons cooking oil and 3 large skinless, boneless chicken breast halves cut into 1 inch pieces. Keep the large pot handy for the stovetop.
The chicken is cut into 1 inch pieces. Should I season it before it hits the pot, or wait?
Wait until after it starts browning in the pot. For now, also have sea salt to taste and 1 tablespoon chili powder, or more to taste, within reach.
Oil, chicken, sea salt, and chili powder are ready. What heat should the pot be on?
Pour the oil into the large pot and heat it over medium heat until it looks loose and shimmery.
The oil is shimmering. Do I add all the chicken at once?
Add the chicken pieces to the pot and brown them on all sides. Try to keep them in a single layer as much as you can so they brown instead of steaming.
The chicken is mostly browned, with a little color on the edges. Is this when the spices go in?
Yes. Season the chicken with sea salt, chili powder, cumin, ground chipotle, black pepper, and cayenne pepper, stirring so the pieces get evenly coated.
It smells good and the seasoning is coating the chicken. I have onion and both bell peppers chopped—when do those go in?
Mix in the onion, green bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper right into the pot with the seasoned chicken.
Should I scrape up the browned bits while I stir the vegetables in?
Yes, stir and scrape the bottom of the pot as the onion, green bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper mix in. That keeps the chili base flavorful and helps nothing stick.

Got it. I’m clearing counter space—what ingredients should be out before I heat anything?
Pull out 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 2 teaspoons baking soda, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Keep a sifter or fine sieve nearby.
I have the dry goods. The chocolate is still wrapped—how much am I chopping?
Chop 6 (1 ounce) squares of unsweetened chocolate into small pieces so they’ll be ready when the batter needs them.
Chocolate is chopped. Should the oven be on before I deal with the pans?
Yes, set the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) so it can come up to temperature while you prepare the pans.
The oven is heating. I have two round pans—what size and coating do they need?
Grease and flour 2 (9 inch) pans, covering the bottoms and sides so the cake releases cleanly.
The pans are coated, but flour dust is everywhere. Before I wipe up, what happens with the dry mix?
Sift together the flour, baking soda, and salt; this evens out the leavening and breaks up clumps.
After sifting, do I stir the chopped chocolate into that bowl?
Not in this listed step. Once the flour, baking soda, and salt are sifted together, set that mixture aside.
So right now I have chopped chocolate waiting, pans ready, oven heating, and dry ingredients resting—anything else from this section?

That’s the full setup from this part: 2 greased and floured 9 inch pans, the oven at 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), 6 (1 ounce) squares of unsweetened chocolate chopped, and the sifted flour mixture set aside.

The butter is soft and the sugar is measured. Do I need anything else before mixing?
Yes—keep 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and 2 cups all-purpose flour nearby. You’ll add the vanilla before the flour.
Everything is measured. Should the butter and sugar look fluffy, or just combined?
Cream the softened butter with the confectioners' sugar in the mixing bowl until the mixture looks smooth and light, with no dry sugar pockets.
It’s pale and creamy now. I don’t want to overdo the vanilla—how much goes in?
Add 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and mix just until it’s worked evenly through the butter-sugar mixture.

Add the 2 cups all-purpose flour gradually, mixing as you go, until the dough comes together evenly.

Lightly flour your hands, then scoop tablespoonfuls of batter and shape them into cookies.
I’m setting them on the tray for serving later. Any last texture cue before I move on?
They should look evenly shaped and tender, with the dough handled just enough to form the shortbread logs without compacting them.
I want to make Banana Chip Muffins I. Can you help me get set up without rushing through the mixing?

Absolutely. Put a large bowl on the counter for the dry ingredients and a small bowl nearby for the egg mixture. For the dry bowl, measure out 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 cup white sugar, 1 tablespoon baking powder, and 1/2 teaspoon salt.
The flour and sugar are measured. Should the baking powder and salt go in with them right away?
Yes, add the 1 tablespoon baking powder and 1/2 teaspoon salt to that same large bowl. The recipe also has you measure the chocolate chips into the large bowl with the dry ingredients.
Chocolate chips are in too. Do I stir this a lot or just combine it?
Mix the dry ingredients thoroughly so the baking powder and salt are evenly spread through the flour and sugar. Once it looks even, make a well in the center of the mixture.
I made the well. What bowl do I use for the egg?
Use the small bowl. Crack in the egg and beat it until it looks frothy, with small bubbles and a lighter texture.
The egg is frothy now. I have bananas, milk, and cooking oil ready, but the recipe doesn't show amounts here.
That's fine—use the amounts called for in your full recipe if you have them. At this point, mix the cooking oil, milk, and bananas into the beaten egg.
Should the bananas be totally smooth before I mix them in?
They can be mashed smooth or left with a few small soft bits, depending on the muffin texture you like. Stir them into the egg mixture with the milk and cooking oil until everything is combined.
Wet mixture is combined. Do I pour it into the well in the dry bowl now?
Yes. Pour the banana, milk, cooking oil, and egg mixture into the well you made in the dry ingredients, then gently mix from the center outward until the batter comes together.

messages.content: I’m teaching empanadas in a hands-on pastry workshop today, so I need the traditional classroom approach for this batch. Can you guide me that way?
For this workshop batch, make the dough with the wheat flour so the empanadas have the traditional structure students can handle and shape.
Perfect, just for today’s class. What should I have measured before the students come up to the table?
Set out 1/2 cup softened butter and 1 (3 ounce) package cream cheese first. They need to be soft enough to cream together smoothly.
Those are ready, and I’ve got a mixing bowl at each station. What else belongs on the tray?
Add 1 cup sifted all-purpose flour and 1 cup fruit preserves to the setup. Keep the preserves aside for later filling; the flour goes into the dough.
For the make-ahead part, should I demonstrate the dough mixing before talking about chilling?
Yes. Explain that this dough starts the day before: cream the softened butter and cream cheese together until the mixture is smoothly blended.
What should the students look for before adding the flour?
Have them check that there are no obvious streaks of butter or cream cheese. Once it looks smooth and unified, beat in the 1 cup sifted all-purpose flour.
If the dough comes together, how should they package it for the overnight rest?
Shape the dough into a smooth ball, then wrap it well in foil or cling wrap so it doesn’t dry out in the refrigerator.
How long can I tell them it may stay chilled if they prep it ahead?
It should be refrigerated overnight, and it can stay wrapped and chilled for up to a week before baking day.
On baking day, when should I bring the dough out for the class to roll and fill?
Take the dough out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before using it, so it softens enough for students to handle without losing its shape.
I want to make Dads Flat Bread this afternoon. Can you guide me without rushing through the dough stages?
Absolutely. Set out 1 (.25 ounce) package active dry yeast and 2 cups warm water, divided. Aim for the water to be 110 to 115 degrees so the yeast wakes up without being overheated.
I have the yeast and I’m checking the water temperature now. What should be on the counter with it?
You’ll also need 1/3 cup sugar and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil. Keep your large mixing bowl ready, plus flour for the dough and for dusting the work surface later.
The bowl is out. Do I use all the water with the yeast?
Use only 1/2 cup of the warm water at this point. Pour it into the large mixing bowl and dissolve the yeast in it, stirring gently until it’s evenly mixed.
The yeast is dissolved in the 1/2 cup. It looks a little cloudy but smooth.
That’s right. Add the sugar, vegetable oil, salt, rye or whole wheat flour, 3 cups all-purpose flour, and the remaining warm water. Beat the mixture until it looks smooth rather than streaky or dry.
I’ve mixed that in. The batter is thick, but it’s not quite holding together like dough yet.
Add more all-purpose flour gradually, just enough to bring it into a soft dough. Stop once it gathers together and feels workable, not stiff or overly dry.
It’s forming a soft dough now. Should I flour the counter heavily?
Dust the surface lightly at first, then add a little more only if the dough sticks. Turn the dough out onto the floured surface and get ready to knead.
The dough is on the counter and sticking just a bit to my hands. How long am I kneading?
Knead until the dough becomes smooth and elastic, about 6 to 8 minutes. If it keeps sticking, use small sprinkles of flour rather than dumping a lot on at once.

I’m making Black Bean Chili and have a large saucepan out. Can you guide me from prep through cooking?
Absolutely. Set out 1 tablespoon olive oil, 1 chopped onion, 2 red bell peppers that are seeded and chopped, and 1 jalapeno pepper that’s seeded and minced.
The onion and peppers are chopped. Should I heat the pan before adding anything?
Yes. Put the large saucepan over medium-high heat and add the olive oil so it can warm up.
The oil is shimmering a little. I also see mushrooms, tomatoes, and corn ready on the counter—do they go in with the peppers?
They do. Add the onion, red bell peppers, jalapeno, mushrooms, tomatoes, and corn to the saucepan.
Everything is in the saucepan. How long should I cook this mixture?
Sautee it for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onions look translucent.
The onions are turning translucent and the vegetables have softened. What seasoning goes in?
Sprinkle in black pepper, cumin, and chili powder, then stir so the vegetables are evenly coated.
The spices are mixed in and it smells good. What should I add to make it more like chili?
Stir in the black beans, chicken broth, and salt, making sure the beans are distributed through the seasoned vegetables.
The beans and broth are in. Should I keep it on medium-high or adjust anything while it comes together?
Keep it moving gently in the saucepan and let the beans, broth, salt, and seasoned vegetables combine; once it’s hot throughout, it’s ready to serve.
I'm making Chicken and Herbs in White Wine and want to keep it organized. What should I set out before I turn on the stove?
Set out 2 tablespoons olive oil and 1 chicken, about 4 pounds, cut into pieces. You’ll also want garlic powder nearby so you can season the chicken right before browning.
Got the chicken pieces and oil out. Are the mushrooms part of the early prep too?
Yes. Have 1/2 pound fresh mushrooms sliced and ready. The recipe starts with the chicken, but having the mushrooms prepped will keep the cooking moving smoothly.
I have a large Dutch oven on the stove. Should the oil go in before it heats?
Add the olive oil to the large Dutch oven, then heat it over medium heat. Give the oil a moment to warm so the chicken can brown instead of just sitting in cool oil.
The oil looks glossy now. Do I season every piece of chicken before it goes in?
Sprinkle the chicken pieces with garlic powder to taste before browning. Add them to the Dutch oven in a way that gives the pieces contact with the hot surface.
Some pieces are crowded. Is it okay if they overlap a little while browning?
Try not to overlap them much. The goal is to brown the chicken on both sides, so each piece needs enough surface contact to pick up color.
Both sides are browned now. Where should I put the chicken while I deal with the pan?
Move the browned chicken to paper towels. That gives you a place to rest it while you handle the fat in the Dutch oven.
There’s a good amount of rendered fat left in the pot. What do I do with that before continuing?
Spoon off the chicken fat, then return the pan to the stove. Keep your sliced mushrooms close by for the next part of the recipe.

messages.content: I want to make Cheddar Artichoke Quiche Cups—can you guide me while I prep?
Absolutely. Start by setting out 1 (7.5 ounce) jar of marinated artichoke hearts, 1 small onion finely chopped, 1 minced garlic clove, and 4 beaten eggs.
I’ve got the jar open. Should I dump out all the marinade or save some?
Drain the artichoke hearts, but keep half of the marinade. You’ll use that saved marinade to cook the onion and garlic.
Got it. The artichokes are drained and I saved half the liquid. Do I need to cut them small?
Yes, chop the artichoke hearts into small pieces so they’ll distribute evenly through the quiche cups, then set them aside.

Use a skillet. Add the reserved marinade, then sauté the chopped onion and minced garlic in it until they’re tender.
How soft should the onion be before I stop cooking it?
Cook it until the onion looks softened and no longer sharp or crunchy, and the garlic smells fragrant. Once they’re tender, take the skillet off the heat and set the mixture aside.
The skillet mixture is cooling. What goes into the bowl with the eggs?
In a large bowl, combine the beaten eggs with bread crumbs, mustard, oregano, pepper, and hot pepper sauce.
Should I add the chopped artichokes and the onion-garlic mixture to that bowl too?
Yes, fold the chopped artichokes and the sautéed onion-garlic mixture into the egg mixture so everything is evenly combined before portioning the quiche cups.

Cover the dish and refrigerate it to marinate for at least 2 hours, or overnight if you have that much time.

messages.content: I’m making Eggplant Mixed Grill and want to stay organized. Can you guide me through the prep?

Absolutely. Set out 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh oregano, and 2 tablespoons chopped fresh basil. You’ll also need a large resealable plastic bag for the marinade.
The herbs and oil are on the counter. Should I mix the marinade right in the bag?

Yes. In the large resealable plastic bag, combine the olive oil, parsley, oregano, basil, vinegar, kosher salt, pepper, and garlic. Seal it briefly and gently shake or massage the bag so the seasonings are evenly mixed.
The marinade is mixed. I have onion, asparagus, mushrooms, eggplant, and both red and yellow bell peppers ready.
Add the onion, asparagus, mushrooms, eggplant, red bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper directly into the bag with the marinade. Try to spread them out a bit so the oil and herbs can coat everything.
They’re in the bag, but it’s pretty full. What’s the best way to coat them without making a mess?

Seal the bag tightly, leaving just a little room for the vegetables to move. Turn the bag over several times and gently massage the outside so the marinade reaches the eggplant, mushrooms, asparagus, onion, and peppers.
Everything looks coated. How long does it need to sit, and where should I put it?
Put the sealed bag in the refrigerator to marinate for 2 hours. Turn it occasionally during that time so the vegetables keep redistributing through the marinade.
The 2 hours are almost up. Should I start heating the grill now?
Yes, preheat the grill for high heat while the vegetables finish marinating. That way the grate is hot and ready when you take the bag out of the refrigerator.
The grill is hot. Anything I should do before the vegetables go on?
Lightly oil the grill grate before adding the marinated vegetables. That helps reduce sticking, especially with the eggplant and peppers.
Can you help me make Chicken with Vegetables in the slow cooker today?
Absolutely. Set out your slow cooker, then gather 1 cup sliced fresh mushrooms, 4 chicken drumsticks with the skin removed, 4 chicken thighs with the skin removed, and 4 sliced celery ribs.
The slow cooker is on the counter, and I have the mushrooms, drumsticks, thighs, and celery ready. Should the chicken go in whole?
Yes, keep the drumsticks and thighs whole. Place the sliced mushrooms in the slow cooker along with all the chicken pieces.
The mushrooms and chicken are in. I see celery in the recipe, but it also mentions other vegetables—what should I add with it?
Add the sliced celery, zucchini, carrots, and onion over the chicken and mushrooms so the vegetables cook down around the meat.
Vegetables are layered in. What liquids and seasonings go in before I cover it?
Pour in the tomato juice and broth, then add the garlic, paprika, and pepper. Try to distribute the seasonings across the top rather than leaving them in one spot.
Everything is added. Should I stir it, or leave the chicken pieces where they are?
You can leave the chicken pieces settled in place. If you want, gently nudge the vegetables and liquid around them, but there’s no need for a full stir.
Got it. What setting and how long should this cook?
Cover the slow cooker and cook on low for 5 hours, or until the chicken is done and the meat juices run clear.
After the 5 hours, how do I handle it for serving without it cooling too fast?
Remove the chicken and vegetables from the slow cooker and keep them warm until serving. Spoon some of the cooking juices over the top if you’d like to keep everything moist.
Can you help me make Dilly Chicken and Potatoes? I’ve got a large skillet out and want to make sure I prep everything in the right order.
Absolutely. Start by getting the main ingredients ready: 1 broiler-fryer chicken, about 3 1/2 pounds, cut up, and 1 pound of new potatoes cut into chunks.
The chicken is cut up and the potatoes are chunked. Do I need anything else by the stove before I turn on the heat?
Yes—keep 2 tablespoons of cooking oil nearby, along with 1 cup half-and-half cream. You’ll also need salt and pepper for the cream mixture later.
Got it. Should the skillet be hot before the chicken and potatoes go in?
Set the large skillet over medium heat, add the oil, then put in the chicken and potatoes once the oil is heated.
They’re in the pan now. How long am I browning them, and what should I watch for?
Brown the chicken and potatoes in the oil for 10 to 15 minutes, turning the pieces so they get color instead of just sitting on one side.
The potatoes have some color and the chicken is browned on the outside. Do I leave everything in while making the sauce?
No, lift the chicken and potatoes out of the skillet and set them aside for the moment.
They’re on a plate. There’s a decent amount of fat and browned bits in the skillet—how much should stay?
Pour off the excess drippings, but keep 1 tablespoon in the skillet so the cream has something flavorful to mix with.
I saved about 1 tablespoon. How do I bring the cream into it without making a mess?
Add the 1 cup half-and-half cream to the drippings, then season with salt and pepper. Stir everything together until the cream and drippings are mixed smoothly.
Can you guide me through making Drunken Fruit Salsa? I’ve got a cutting board out and want to prep everything neatly.
Absolutely. Start by peeling 1 medium mango and finely dicing it. Put the pieces in a glass bowl if you have one, since the fruit will chill with rum later.
The mango is diced. I also have strawberries washed—how much should I chop?
Chop 3/4 cup fresh strawberries into small pieces, about the same size as the mango, so the salsa scoops evenly.
Done. I’ve got a kiwi here too; should it be tiny dice like the mango?
Yes. Peel 1 kiwi and finely dice it, then add it to the bowl with the mango and strawberries.
The fruit is all in the bowl. I’m handling the jalapeno now—what’s the best prep for it?
Seed 1 jalapeno pepper, then finely chop it. Add it to the fruit; the small cut helps spread the heat without big spicy bites.
Jalapeno is mixed in. The recipe mentions mint and rum—do those go in right away?
Yes, stir the mango, strawberries, kiwi, jalapeno, mint, and rum together in the glass bowl until everything looks evenly coated.
It smells great. Should I serve it now or let it sit?
Refrigerate it for 1 to 3 hours so the flavors can mingle. Stir it once or twice while it chills.
If I’m serving it after the full chill time, what texture should I check for?
Look for glossy fruit with some juices gathered at the bottom, but not mushy pieces. Give it one gentle stir before serving so the rum, mint, jalapeno, and fruit are evenly distributed.

Sure. We’ll keep the recipe’s original amounts and add practical metric notes where they help: 1 cup chopped peeled mango, about 165 g; 1/4 cup chopped red onion, about 40 g; 1/4 cup minced fresh cilantro, roughly 4 g; and 1/4 cup lime juice, about 60 ml.
Great. I’ve got a bowl out and the mango is peeled. How small should I chop it?
Chop the peeled mango into small bite-size pieces so it scoops easily with chips or sits nicely on fish or tacos. Measure out 1 cup, about 165 g, and add it to the bowl.
Mango is in. The red onion is pretty sharp—how much goes in?
Use the recipe amount: 1/4 cup chopped red onion, about 40 g. Chop it fairly fine so it spreads through the salsa without taking over, then add it to the mango.
Yes, this side-by-side measuring is exactly how I like to cook from recipes. What’s next?
Add 1/4 cup minced fresh cilantro, roughly 4 g. Give it a quick mince so you don’t get big leafy clumps, then scatter it into the bowl.
Cilantro is in. I’m squeezing limes now—what amount am I aiming for?
You want 1/4 cup lime juice, which is about 60 ml. Pour it over the mango, onion, and cilantro.
Everything is in the bowl. Should I stir hard or keep it gentle?
Fold it together gently until the lime juice coats everything and the onion and cilantro are evenly mixed through the mango. Try not to mash the mango pieces.
It looks mixed. Do I serve it right away or wait?
Let it stand for 30 minutes before serving. That rest gives the lime juice time to mingle with the mango, onion, and cilantro.
While it rests, should I cover it or leave it uncovered on the counter?
Cover the bowl while it stands. After the 30 minutes, give it one gentle stir, taste the texture and balance, and serve the Gingered Mango Salsa.

For your weeknight version, swap the butter with olive oil or plant-based butter, use unsweetened oat milk in place of dairy milk-style liquid, and bring back the creamy Alfredo feel with dairy-free cheese or a cashew-style sauce.

That will make this quick. Measure the original amounts as your guide: 1 pint for the creamy liquid, 1/2 cup for the butter component, and 1 1/2 cups for the grated cheese component. Set the dairy-free versions right next to the pan so they go in together.

Use plant-based butter if you want it closer to the original 1/2 cup butter richness. Olive oil works too, but it will taste a little lighter and less classic Alfredo-like.
Perfect, that’s why these swaps are my go-to for keeping dinner simple.

Great—put the saucepan over medium-low heat and add the creamy liquid, the plant-based butter, and the dairy-free Parmesan or cashew-style creamy element all at once, just like the recipe combines the whipping cream, butter or margarine, and grated Parmesan cheese.

Stir steadily rather than aggressively. Keep it on medium-low heat and let the plant-based butter melt into the creamy base while the dairy-free cheese or cashew-style sauce smooths out.
It looks a little thin right now. Should I raise the heat?
Keep it at medium-low. The recipe’s key cue is to cook until smooth, not to boil it down fast. A gentle heat helps the sauce come together without separating.

Take the saucepan off the heat. That matches the next part of the recipe, and it also protects the creamy texture once it has smoothed out.

Let it stand briefly, because the sauce thickens as it sits. Once it has the texture you like, toss it with the pasta and serve while it’s still warm.

messages.content: I’m making Chicken Pot Pie II and want to get the chicken portion started. What should I set out?
Set out 1 1/2 pounds of skinless, boneless chicken breast meat, 1 cup chicken broth, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon ground black pepper. You’ll also need a large saucepan with a lid.

Put the chicken meat and the 1 cup chicken broth into the large saucepan together, then add the salt and ground black pepper.

Place the saucepan over medium-high heat. Let the broth heat with the chicken and seasonings until it comes to a boil.

Give it another minute or two on medium-high. Once it reaches a boil, reduce the heat to low so it can simmer gently.

Yes, cover the saucepan with the lid and keep it on a low simmer. Let it cook for 30 minutes, or until the chicken is no longer pink in the center and the juices run clear.

Open the lid carefully and check the thickest piece. It should not be pink in the center, and the juices should run clear. If it still looks pink, cover it again and simmer a little longer.
The chicken looks cooked through and the juices are clear. What should I do with it now?
Remove the chicken from the saucepan and let it cool before handling it further for the pot pie.

Use 1 egg, beaten, and 1/4 cup milk. Keep them near a large mixing bowl for the filling.

Boil the cabbage leaves for 2 minutes, then drain them well. Lay them out so they’re easier to fill.

Combine 1 cup cooked rice, the beaten egg, 1/4 cup milk, onion, ground beef, salt, and pepper in the large bowl. Mix it until the ingredients are evenly distributed.

Spoon about 1/4 cup of the meat mixture into the center of each cabbage leaf. Don’t overfill them, since you’ll need room to tuck the ends in.

Roll each cabbage leaf around the filling, tucking in the ends as you go so the meat mixture stays enclosed. Repeat with all 12 leaves.

Great. I want the students to set up their stations before we touch the chicken. What should each station have?
Have each station set out 4 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves, 1 cup milk, 1 cup dry bread crumbs, and 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese.
Should the milk be in a bowl or something wider for soaking?
Use a shallow dish wide enough to hold the thin chicken pieces in a layer, because the milk needs to cover them evenly once they’re cut and pounded.
We have cutting boards ready. How should I demo the slicing so they get even pieces?
Lay each breast flat and slice it horizontally into thirds. From the 4 chicken breast halves, that gives you 12 thin chicken fillets.
If a few pieces come out uneven, do I fix that before the milk soak?
Yes. Lightly pound each piece after slicing so the fillets are more even, but keep it gentle so they stay intact.
What should I tell them about the texture after pounding?
They should look thin and fairly uniform, not torn or mashed. The goal is even thickness so the pieces handle the breading well later.
Once they’re pounded, do they go straight into the dish with milk?
Exactly. Place the chicken pieces in the dish, then pour the 1 cup milk over them so the surfaces are moistened.
How long should I build into the class schedule for that soak?
Let the chicken soak for 10 minutes. While they wait, the class can combine or organize the 1 cup dry bread crumbs and 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese for the next part.

Absolutely. Set out 1 cup semisweet chocolate chips and 1/2 cup softened butter. You’ll also want a heavy saucepan for melting the chocolate gently.
The saucepan is out, and the butter is soft. What sugars should I measure before I turn on the heat?
Measure 1/2 cup white sugar and 1/2 cup packed brown sugar. Keep them near the softened butter so you can cream them together after the chocolate is melted.
I’ve got both sugars measured. Should I start with the chocolate chips in the pan?
Yes. Put the semisweet chocolate chips into the heavy saucepan and keep the heat very low so they melt slowly without scorching.
They’re starting to soften around the edges. Do I leave them alone or stir?
Stir them gently as they melt so the chocolate becomes smooth and even throughout.
The chocolate looks smooth now. What texture am I looking for with the butter and sugars?
Cream the softened butter with the white sugar and packed brown sugar until the mixture looks lighter and fluffier than when you started.
It’s lighter and a bit fluffy. I’m ready for the next mixing part.
Beat in the eggs one at a time, mixing each one in before adding the next.
Should I scrape the bowl while adding the eggs?
Yes, scrape down the sides as needed so the eggs blend evenly into the creamed butter and sugars.
I want to make Grandmas Gnocchi today. Can you guide me while I get set up?
Absolutely. Put out 6 russet potatoes, 1 cup all-purpose flour, 1 lightly beaten egg, and 1 tablespoon olive oil. You’ll also want a large pot for boiling and a fork for mashing later.
The potatoes are on the counter, and I’ve got the flour measured. Should I start heating water before dealing with the egg and oil?
Yes. Fill a large pot with water, salt it well, and bring it to a boil. While it heats, you can lightly beat the egg and keep the olive oil nearby.
The water is starting to simmer, not quite boiling yet. Do the potatoes go in whole?
For this recipe, drop the russet potatoes into the salted water once it reaches a full boil. Cook them until they’re tender but still firm, about 15 minutes.
They’ve been boiling for a while. How do I know if they’re tender but not falling apart?
Pierce one with a fork or knife. It should go in without much resistance, but the potato should still hold together instead of crumbling in the water.
That texture seems right, and the timer is around 15 minutes. What should I do at the sink?
Drain the potatoes carefully, then let them cool just enough to handle. Once they’re warm rather than scorching hot, peel off the skins.
They’re peeled and still warm. Should I add the flour, egg, and oil now?
Before combining anything else, season the potatoes with salt and mash them with a fork. Keep the mash as even as you can so the gnocchi base starts smooth.
The potatoes are salted and mashed. Is that the end of the written steps for this part?
Yes, that completes the listed prep: the potatoes have been boiled in salted water, cooked about 15 minutes, drained, cooled slightly, peeled, seasoned with salt, and mashed with a fork.
I want to make the Awesome Turkey Sandwich for lunch. Can you guide me without making a big mess?
Absolutely. Set out 2 slices of whole wheat bread, toasted if you like, plus a plate or cutting board and a butter knife for spreading.
The bread is toasted and on a plate. What spreads should I measure out?
Use 1 tablespoon mayonnaise for one slice and 2 teaspoons Dijon-style prepared mustard for the other slice.
I’ve got the mayo and Dijon ready. Should I put them on before the turkey?
Yes. Spread the mayonnaise across one slice of toast, then spread the Dijon mustard across the other slice so each piece is evenly covered.
Both slices are coated. I have the smoked turkey open—how much goes on?
Lay 3 slices of smoked turkey breast on one side, keeping the slices fairly even so the sandwich stacks neatly.
The turkey is on. The recipe mentions guacamole too—does that go straight on the meat?
It does. Spread the guacamole over the turkey in a thin, even layer so it helps hold the toppings in place.
Guacamole is spread. I’m adding the fresh toppings now; what order makes sense?
Pile on the salad greens, bean sprouts, avocado, and cheese. Keep the pile centered so the sandwich is easier to close.
It’s stacked pretty high. Any trick for serving it without everything sliding out?
Place the mustard-coated slice on top, press gently with your palm, then cut the sandwich in half if you want it easier to handle.

messages.content: I’m cooking Fiery Fish Tacos with Crunchy Corn Salsa for a backyard cookout this afternoon, so I want the outdoor version today. Can you guide me while I prep?
Absolutely—since this is for the cookout, go with the outdoor grill or smoker approach for this batch.
Great, I’ve got a cutting board and a big bowl out. Which salsa ingredients should I measure first?
Start with the corn and onion: measure 1 cup corn, then add 1/2 cup diced red onion to your prep area.
The onion is diced, and the corn is ready. What crunchy pieces come next?
Bring in 1 cup peeled, chopped jicama for crunch, plus 1/2 cup diced red bell pepper for sweetness and color.
Nice. Should I heat the grill before mixing the salsa, or wait until the bowl is done?
Get the grill preheating for high heat now so it’s ready when you need it.

In a medium bowl, mix together the corn, red onion, jicama, red bell pepper, and cilantro.

Stir in the lime juice and lime zest, folding gently so the vegetables stay crisp.
That smells great. I also need the spicy seasoning ready before people start asking for tacos.
In a small bowl, combine the cayenne pepper, ground black pepper, and salt.
Should that seasoning stay separate from the salsa while I set up the serving table?
Yes, keep the spice mixture separate and the corn salsa chilled or shaded until serving; then you’ll have the bright crunchy topping and the fiery seasoning ready for the fish tacos.

messages.content: I want to make A Very Intense Fruit Smoothie—can you guide me while I set up the blender?

Absolutely. Put your blender jar on the base and have the lid ready. You’ll need 1 (10 ounce) package frozen mixed berries, 1 (15 ounce) can sliced peaches that has been drained, and 2 tablespoons honey.
The berries are still frozen, and I drained the peaches. Should the peaches go in with the syrup or without it?
Use the drained peaches without the syrup. Add the frozen mixed berries, the drained sliced peaches, and the honey directly to the blender jar.
The honey is sticking to the spoon a bit. Is that okay, or should I scrape it in?
Scrape in as much of the 2 tablespoons honey as you can so the smoothie gets the intended sweetness. A small silicone spatula or another spoon works well.
Everything is in the blender. Do I need any liquid to get it moving?
For this recipe, don’t add extra liquid yet—the listed ingredients are just the frozen mixed berries, drained peaches, and honey. Secure the lid and start blending.
It’s blending, but the frozen berries are making it kind of chunky near the top.
Pause the blender, remove the lid only after the blades stop, and push the fruit down with a spatula. Put the lid back on and blend again until the mixture looks smooth.
Now it’s moving better. What texture am I aiming for before I pour it?
Aim for an even, smooth texture with no visible peach slices or berry pieces. If you still see chunks, blend a little longer.
It looks smooth now. Should I serve it right away?
Yes, pour it into glasses right away while it’s cold and thick. Give the blender jar a quick rinse soon after serving so the honey and fruit don’t dry onto it.
I’m making Baked Fake Steak with Gravy. Can you help me get set up before I start mixing?
Absolutely. Set out 3 pounds ground beef, 17 saltine crackers finely crushed, 1/2 cup milk, and 1 1/2 teaspoons garlic powder. You’ll also want onion powder, salt, and pepper for seasoning.
The beef is in the fridge and I’ve got the crackers. Should I crush all 17 pretty fine?
Yes, crush all 17 saltines finely so they blend evenly into the beef mixture rather than leaving big cracker pieces.
Got it. What bowl and pan should I grab?
Use a large mixing bowl for the beef mixture, and get a 10x15 inch jellyroll pan ready for shaping it later.
The bowl is out. Do I add the milk with the beef right away?
Yes. Put the 3 pounds ground beef in the large bowl, add the finely crushed saltines, and pour in the 1/2 cup milk. Mix those together until the crackers and milk are worked through the meat.
It’s combined, but I haven’t seasoned it yet. How much garlic powder goes in?
Sprinkle in 1 1/2 teaspoons garlic powder, then add onion powder, salt, and pepper. Mix again until the seasoning is well blended throughout.
The texture looks even now. What do I do with the pan?
Line the 10x15 inch jellyroll pan with waxed paper, smoothing it into the corners so the beef mixture can be pressed in evenly.
The waxed paper is in place. How firmly should I pack the meat mixture?
Transfer the beef mixture into the lined pan and press it firmly across the pan, keeping the thickness as even as you can from edge to edge.
Can you help me make Black Bean and Corn Quesadillas? I’m starting with the filling and want to get the prep right.

Absolutely. Set a large saucepan on the stove and gather 2 teaspoons olive oil, 3 tablespoons finely chopped onion, 1 (15.5 ounce) can black beans that are drained and rinsed, and 1 (10 ounce) can whole kernel corn that’s drained.
The beans are rinsed and the corn is drained. Should the onion be very small pieces?
Yes, finely chopped is best so it softens quickly and blends into the beans and corn. Once the onion is ready, heat the 2 teaspoons olive oil in the large saucepan over medium heat.
The oil is heating. How do I know when it’s ready for the onion?
When the oil looks a little shimmery and moves easily across the pan, stir in the 3 tablespoons finely chopped onion.
The onion is in. I don’t want it browned—what texture am I aiming for?
Cook it just until softened, about 2 minutes, stirring so it doesn’t catch or brown too much.
It’s softened and smells good. Do the beans and corn go in together?

Yes. Stir in the drained and rinsed black beans and the drained whole kernel corn, then add the sugar, salsa, and pepper flakes. Mix everything well so the seasonings and salsa coat the filling evenly.
I’ve mixed it all. The salsa made it a little saucy—is that okay?
That’s fine. Keep it over medium heat and cook until the mixture is heated through, about 3 minutes, stirring occasionally.
After those 3 minutes, should the filling be thick enough for quesadillas?

Yes, it should be hot and cohesive, with the beans and corn evenly mixed. If there’s a little extra moisture, give it a final stir and let it sit briefly off the heat before spooning it into the quesadillas.

If you have other cooked leftovers from the meal, cool them promptly, portion them into shallow containers, refrigerate them, and warm those gently later so their texture stays pleasant; the mayonnaise dressing itself should stay cold.
I’ve got a small jar with a tight lid on the counter. What ingredients should I measure into it?
Measure 1/2 cup mayonnaise into the jar, then add 3 teaspoons milk. Those two make the creamy base, so try to measure the milk rather than splash it in.
The mayonnaise and milk are in. I’m checking the seasonings now.
Add 1/4 teaspoon salt and 1 pinch ground black pepper. Scrape down the inside of the jar if mayonnaise is clinging to the sides.
That’s exactly the kind of home-cooking guidance I like—storage notes and whether anything should be reheated later. What do I do with the jar now?
Put the tight-fitting lid on firmly. Hold the jar with one hand over the lid and one around the base so it doesn’t leak when you shake it.
Lid is secure. How vigorous are we talking, and how long should I shake?

Shake it vigorously until the mayonnaise, milk, salt, and pepper look fully combined into a smooth dressing. Since it’s a small amount, you’re mainly looking for an even, pourable texture rather than a set time.
It looks creamy but a little thick on the sides of the jar.

Give the jar a quick scrape or tap to pull the thicker bits down, then shake once more. The recipe keeps the liquid at 3 teaspoons milk, so don’t thin it further unless you decide you want a looser dressing.
The salad is in a bowl and ready. Should I pour all of it on?
Pour the dressing over your salad a little at a time and toss, stopping when the leaves are coated the way you like. Any dressing you don’t use can stay in the jar with the lid on.
I used part of it and there’s some left in the jar. How should I wrap up cleanup and storage?

Wipe the rim, tighten the lid, and refrigerate the leftover dressing promptly. Keep it cold rather than reheating it; if you later serve it with warm leftovers, reheat those gently on their own and add the dressing after.

That works. I’ve got a medium bowl out and the chicken is still in the fridge—what should go into the bowl first?

Add the ketchup, unsweetened pineapple juice, molasses, and your 2 tablespoons of non-alcoholic rum substitute to the medium bowl. The original glaze also includes mustard and garlic, so add those now too if you have them ready.
The glaze looks thick and glossy. Should I season it before it goes on the chicken?
Yes, season the glaze with salt and pepper to taste, then mix it well so the molasses and ketchup are fully blended with the juice, mustard, garlic, and substitute liquid.
Perfect—this is exactly how I like to handle dishes like this, so I don’t have to make a separate pan for the kids.
Great. Lightly oil a 9x13 inch baking dish, then place the chicken pieces in it with a little space between them so the glaze can coat the surfaces evenly.
The baking dish is oiled. Do I pour the glaze over everything or brush it on?
Brush the glaze onto both sides of the chicken pieces, using about 1/2 of the prepared glaze for this stage. Save the rest for later in the cooking process if you plan to baste.
I used roughly half, and the chicken is coated. Do I need to cover the dish before it chills?
Cover the dish before refrigerating so the chicken can marinate without drying out or picking up fridge odors.
How long should I leave it in the fridge if dinner is later tonight?
Marinate it for at least 2 hours. If your schedule allows, overnight is also fine and will give the glaze more time to flavor the chicken.
I can give it a little over 2 hours. Anything I should clean up or save before it goes in?
Wipe the rim of the dish if it got sticky, keep the reserved glaze covered separately, and refrigerate the covered chicken until you’re ready to cook it.

messages.content: Can you guide me through Baked Pork Chops Low Fat Version in a way that works for everyone at the table?

Sure. This recipe is centered on 6 trimmed center cut pork chops, a light seasoning, and a crumb coating. If a splash of liquid is needed anywhere for moisture or depth, keep it family-friendly with stock, juice, diluted vinegar, or another non-alcoholic option so you still get brightness without liquor.
Good. I’ve got a rimmed baking sheet and a couple of shallow bowls out—what ingredients should be on the counter?
Set out the 6 center cut pork chops, trimming away any visible fat if that is not done yet. You’ll also want 1 teaspoon garlic powder and 1/2 teaspoon seasoning salt ready for the seasoning step.
The chops are trimmed and dry-looking. What should I use for the dipping setup?

Use one small bowl for the beaten egg and egg substitute mixture. You’ll also need flour for a light dredge and bread crumbs for the outer coating, since the chops get floured, dipped in egg, then coated generously in crumbs.
Yes, that’s the way I usually make it acceptable for the whole household. Before I bread them, should the oven be heating?
Yes—preheat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C, so it is ready by the time the pork chops are coated.
Oven is set to 350. Do I rinse the pork chops before seasoning?

Rinse the pork chops, then pat them dry very well. Once dry, season them with the garlic powder and seasoning salt to taste, using the 1 teaspoon garlic powder and 1/2 teaspoon seasoning salt as your guide.
They’re seasoned. I want the coating to stick but not get heavy—what order should I follow?

Go in this order: dredge each pork chop lightly in flour, shake off the excess, dip it into the beaten egg and egg substitute mixture, then press it into the bread crumbs so the surface is well coated.
Should I crowd all 6 together on the pan, or leave room between them?
Leave a little space between the 6 coated pork chops on the baking sheet so the crumb coating has a better chance to bake evenly instead of steaming where pieces touch.
The bread crumbs are on and the pan is ready. Anything I should check before it goes in?

Look for an even crumb layer and any bare spots you can patch with a bit more bread crumbs. Once they look evenly coated, bake them in the preheated 350 degrees F oven and serve when the pork chops are cooked through and the coating looks set.

Yes. The original ingredient list has 6 russet potatoes, 1 cup all-purpose flour, 1 lightly beaten egg, and 1 tablespoon olive oil; for the egg-free version, swap the egg for a flax egg, chia egg, applesauce, or a similar binder that keeps the dough cohesive without making it too wet.
I’ve got the potatoes on the counter and a big pot out. Should I measure the flour now too?
Go ahead and measure 1 cup all-purpose flour and keep it nearby. Scrub the 6 russet potatoes, and fill the large pot with salted water so it’s ready for the stove.

Use a flax egg or chia egg rather than applesauce here. It will act more like the original lightly beaten egg and won’t add sweetness to the potato dough.
Perfect—that’s the kind of egg-free adjustment I want as our normal way for simple baking projects. The pot is on the burner now.
Bring that large pot of salted water to a full boil before adding the potatoes. Keep the heat high and give yourself space to lower them in safely.
The water is boiling steadily. Do the potatoes go in whole, and how long am I aiming for?
Drop in the potatoes and cook them until tender but still firm, about 15 minutes. You’re looking for a fork to slide in with some resistance, not for them to fall apart.
They’ve cooked for 15 minutes and feel firm-tender. What’s the cleanest way to handle them next?
Drain the potatoes, let them cool just enough to handle, then peel them. Keep a bowl or cutting board ready so the peeled potatoes don’t roll around.
They’re peeled and still warm. Should I add the flour and binder right away?
Season the potatoes with salt first, then mash them with a fork. Once they’re mashed, you can start working in the 1 cup flour and your egg-free binder gradually so the dough doesn’t become gummy.
The mash looks a little uneven, with a few small potato bits. Is that okay before I shape anything?

Yes—use the yolk-cooked custard approach for this batch so it has the structure you need tonight.

Measure 4 cups half-and-half and 1 cup white sugar first. Those go into the saucepan together over low heat.

Yes. Have 11 egg yolks beaten and nearby, plus 1 teaspoon vanilla extract for later after the mixture has chilled.

Keep it low. Stir the half-and-half and sugar in the saucepan until the sugar is dissolving and the mixture is warm, not simmering hard.

Whisk the beaten yolks in gradually while you keep the mixture moving. Cook until it turns into a light custard, and do not let it boil.

It should look slightly thickened and cohesive, like a thin custard that lightly coats as you whisk. Once it reaches that point, take it off the heat.

Let it cool first, then transfer it to the refrigerator and chill it overnight.
After the overnight chill, what do I stir in before serving it for class practice?
Stir the vanilla into the chilled mixture, then add the cream, dark rum, scotch, and vanilla ice cream until everything is blended.

Set out 1 large avocado, peeled and pitted; 2 cloves garlic, minced; 1 lemon, juiced; and 1/4 cup sour cream if you want the creamier version.

Mix just until the herbs and seasonings look evenly distributed. The salt should be incorporated, but you don’t need to beat the mixture once it’s smooth.

messages.content: I'm cooking Baked Aloha Chicken tonight; for this round I care more about exact handling and food safety than cutting down on dishes. Can you walk me through the right way?
Yes. When raw chicken or accurate mixing is involved, use separate clean tools and surfaces, and I’ll note why as we go.
I have the chicken legs out but still wrapped. Before I touch them, what sauce ingredients should I measure?
Measure the sauce ingredients into clean prep containers or straight into a mixing bowl: 1/4 cup lemon juice, 1/4 cup light corn syrup, 2 tablespoons soy sauce, and 1 teaspoon salt.
Those are measured. The recipe also mentions ginger and corn oil; should those go with the sauce?
Yes, keep the ginger and corn oil with the sauce ingredients. Use a clean spoon or whisk for the sauce so it stays separate from anything that will touch raw chicken.
Got it. I also have crushed pineapple in its liquid. Should I open that now or wait?
Open it now and keep the pineapple with its liquid ready, but don’t add it until the first sauce mixture is smooth.
Oven is still cold, and I have an ovenproof glass baking dish set out. What temperature should I use?
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C. While it heats, keep the glass baking dish clean until the chicken legs go in.
The oven is heating. I’m ready to mix, and I want the sauce texture right.
In the bowl, stir together the lemon juice, light corn syrup, soy sauce, salt, ginger, and corn oil until the mixture looks smooth and evenly blended.
The sauce is smooth. The pineapple is still in the can with the juice.
Stir the crushed pineapple and all of its liquid into the sauce. Use the clean sauce utensil, not anything that has touched the raw chicken.
Pineapple is mixed in. How should I handle the chicken legs and sauce without cross-contaminating?

Place the chicken legs in the ovenproof glass baking dish, then pour the sauce over the top. After the chicken is in the dish, wash your hands and any raw-chicken tools before touching other surfaces.
Can you help me make Eileens Spicy Gingerbread Men? I’ve got a large mixing bowl out and want to make sure I start with the right ingredients.
Absolutely. Set out 1/2 cup margarine and 1/2 cup sugar to begin. Those will go into the large bowl together, so it helps if the margarine is soft enough to cream smoothly.
The margarine is softened and the sugar is measured. Do I need the molasses and egg right away too?
Yes, keep 1/2 cup molasses and 1 egg yolk nearby. You’ll add them after the margarine and sugar are creamed.
I separated the yolk and measured the molasses. How smooth should the margarine and sugar look before I add anything else?
Cream the margarine and sugar in the large bowl until the mixture looks even and smooth, with no obvious streaks of margarine. It doesn’t need to be fluffy like cake batter, just well combined.
That looks smooth now. Should I pour in the molasses all at once?
Go ahead and stir in the molasses, then add the egg yolk and mix until the color is fairly uniform. Scrape the sides of the bowl so the sweetener and yolk are fully worked in.
The mixture is glossy and dark. I see the spice list in the recipe—do those get mixed separately first?
Yes. In a separate bowl, combine the flour, salt, baking powder, baking soda, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, and nutmeg. Once those dry ingredients are evenly mixed, blend them into the molasses mixture.
When I add the dry ingredients, am I aiming for a batter or a firmer dough?
Blend until it’s smooth and evenly mixed. For gingerbread men, it should come together more like a dough than a pourable batter, so stop once there are no dry patches.
The dough is mixed and the bowl sides are mostly clean. What should I do before cutting shapes?
Cover the dough and chill it for at least 1 hour. That rest will firm it up so it’s easier to handle and cut into gingerbread men later.
Can you help me make Cheesy Sweet and Savory Spuds? I’ve got a big pot out but haven’t started peeling yet.
Absolutely. Peel and cube 6 Yukon Gold potatoes and 2 sweet potatoes, keeping the pieces fairly even so they cook at the same pace.
The Yukon Golds are peeled; should the sweet potatoes be cubed about the same size?
Yes, cube the 2 sweet potatoes to match the Yukon Gold pieces as closely as you can. Once they’re all cut, put both kinds of potatoes into the large pot.
They’re in the pot now. How much water should I add?
Add enough water to cover the potatoes and sweet potatoes completely. They should be submerged, but you don’t need to fill the pot all the way.
Water is covering them. Do I add the butter or cream before boiling?
Hold off on the 2 tablespoons butter and 1/2 cup heavy cream for now. Put the pot on the stove and bring the water to a boil.
It’s starting to bubble around the edges. Should I wait for a full boil?
Yes, let it come to a full boil. Keep an eye on it so it doesn’t foam over, and adjust the heat if needed.
The pot reached a boil. What should I do next with the potatoes?
Remove the pot from the heat and drain the potatoes and sweet potatoes carefully, using a colander or the pot lid if that’s what you have.
They’re drained and still steaming. What’s the next setup step?
Preheat the oven broiler. While it heats, keep the drained potatoes nearby along with the butter and heavy cream so you’re ready for the next part.

Absolutely. Set out a large mixing bowl and gather the dry ingredients you have listed: 1 cup rye flour, 3/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/4 cup sugar, and 2 1/2 teaspoons baking powder. You’ll also need salt and caraway seeds for the dry mix.
The rye flour and all-purpose flour are measured. Should they both go into the same bowl?
Yes, put both flours into the large bowl together. Add the sugar and baking powder too, then mix in the salt and caraway seeds so the dry ingredients are evenly combined.

Stir the cheese directly into that dry mixture. Toss it through gently so it’s distributed before the wet ingredients go in.

Either grease the muffin cups or line them with paper liners. Spoon the batter into each cup until it’s about 2/3 full, then they’re ready for the next baking step.
